Unit 6

Transform Plate Margins: The Grinding Edges

Transform margins are where two plates slide laterally past each other along networks of strike-slip faults. No crust is created and no crust is destroyed — only displaced. Despite being the “quietest” boundary type in terms of volcanic and topographic activity, transform margins produce some of the world’s most damaging earthquakes because the faults can be very long, highly coupled, and capable of storing enormous amounts of elastic strain before releasing it catastrophically.

Concept 6.1

Continental Transform Faults: The San Andreas System

The Fault You Can See From Space

The San Andreas Fault is arguably the most famous geological feature in North America. It marks the boundary between the Pacific Plate (moving northwest) and the North American Plate (moving roughly west-southwest) over a total length of about 1,300 km, from the Salton Sea in the south to Cape Mendocino in the north. The relative motion is right-lateral (dextral): stand on either side of the fault and the opposite side has moved to your right. The rate of motion is approximately 5 cm/yr — in geological terms, Los Angeles (on the Pacific Plate) is moving toward San Francisco at the pace of a growing fingernail. In about 15 million years, Los Angeles will be a suburb of San Francisco.

From the air or on satellite imagery, the San Andreas is unmistakable. It appears as a linear scar of disrupted topography — ridge lines that are abruptly offset horizontally, stream valleys that are bent at angles where they cross the fault, small pressure ridges and elongated valleys alternating along the fault trace. These geomorphic features are the calling card of a right-lateral strike-slip fault. The offset stream channels can even be used to measure the long-term slip rate: where a stream channel is offset 3 km and dating of offset deposits gives 60,000 years, the rate is 3,000 m / 60,000 yr = 5 cm/yr.

Right-Lateral vs. Left-Lateral: The Definitive Test

Determining the sense of motion on a strike-slip fault requires a marker that was once continuous across the fault and is now offset. Stream channels are ideal markers. Stand in a helicopter above a right-lateral fault and look along the fault trace: streams crossing the fault from your left will be deflected to the right before they continue on the other side. For a left-lateral fault, streams are deflected to the left. Another method: look at offset ridges or road cuts. If the right side of the fault has been displaced toward you relative to the left side, the fault is right-lateral. A mnemonic: for right-lateral faults, your right hand points the direction the opposite side has moved.

Pull-Apart Basins and Restraining Bends: The Complexity of Real Transform Faults

Real transform faults are never perfectly straight. Where the fault bends such that the two plates are locally pulling apart (a releasing bend), extension occurs at the bend, creating a small pull-apart basin. The Salton Sea and Death Valley in California formed as pull-apart basins along releasing bends in the San Andreas system. Where the fault bends such that the plates are locally pushed together (a restraining bend), compression occurs, creating uplifted pressure ridges and small mountain ranges — the Santa Cruz Mountains and the Transverse Ranges near Los Angeles are restraining-bend uplifts along the San Andreas.

The Queen Charlotte Fault: San Andreas’ Canadian Counterpart

Running along the coast of British Columbia, the Queen Charlotte Fault System is a right-lateral transform boundary where the Pacific Plate slides northwest relative to the North American Plate. It accommodates approximately 5–6 cm/yr of motion — nearly identical to the San Andreas. In 2012, the Haida Gwaii earthquake (M7.7) ruptured part of this fault, generating a small tsunami. The Queen Charlotte Fault merges to the south with the Cascadia subduction zone — illustrating that real plate boundaries often transition from one type to another along strike.

Concept 6.2

Oceanic Transform Faults: Why Mid-Ocean Ridges Are Broken Into Segments

If you look at a mid-ocean ridge on a map — the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, for instance — it is not a smooth, continuous structure. It is broken into dozens or hundreds of segments offset laterally by transform faults. Why? The answer lies in the geometry of a spreading ridge on a spherical planet. A straight ridge cannot spread uniformly across a curved surface; the geometry demands that the ridge be broken into short segments connected by transforms that allow each segment to spread along the correct Euler pole direction. Think of how you peel an orange: the peel can’t lie flat without being torn into segments connected by curved cuts. The transforms are those curved connecting cuts.

Active Transform vs. Inactive Fracture Zone: A Critical Distinction

The most commonly confused concept in oceanic transform tectonics. The active transform is only the segment of the fault that lies between the two offset ridge crests — this is where the plates are moving in opposite directions and earthquakes occur. The fracture zone is the extension of this structure beyond the ridge ends into the interior of each plate. On the fracture zone beyond the ridge ends, both sides of the fault are on the same plate and moving in the same direction, so there is no relative motion, no stress buildup, and no earthquakes. The fracture zone is preserved on the seafloor as a topographic scar — a linear trough or ridge — but is seismically dead. Confusing the two is a classic exam error: only the transform segment (between ridges) is active and produces earthquakes; the fracture zone extensions are fossil features.

Unit 7

Hotspots and Mantle Plumes: Volcanism Without a Plate Boundary

About 10% of the world’s volcanism occurs far from any plate boundary — in the middle of plates, often thousands of kilometres from the nearest ridge or subduction zone. This “intraplate volcanism” is explained by mantle plumes: narrow, buoyant columns of unusually hot mantle material rising from deep within the Earth (possibly from the core-mantle boundary, 2,900 km down) that penetrate through the lithosphere and generate persistent volcanic activity at the surface. The surface expression of a plume is called a hotspot. The key characteristic that distinguishes hotspot volcanism from all other types is the age-progressive volcanic chain it leaves as the plate moves over the stationary plume.

Concept 7.1

Plume Mechanism and Global Distribution

How a Mantle Plume Works

A simple analogy: imagine a candle burning below a conveyor belt. The flame (the plume) is stationary. As the belt (the plate) moves across the flame, the material passing directly over the flame is heated and burned — producing a series of marks on the belt in the direction of belt motion, with the oldest marks at the end that has moved furthest from the current position of the flame. This is exactly what a mantle plume does to a tectonic plate. The plume is stationary (or moves much more slowly than the overlying plate); the plate passes over it; wherever the plate is directly above the plume, magma melts through and erupts, creating a volcano. As the plate moves on, that volcano is carried away from the plume and becomes extinct; a new volcano forms above the plume at the new position. The result is an age-progressive chain of extinct, eroded volcanic edifices trailing behind the currently-active volcano like a trail of breadcrumbs.

What Drives the Plume?

The source of the heat that drives mantle plumes is debated, but the leading hypothesis is that plumes originate at the core-mantle boundary (CMB), 2,900 km depth, where heat from the liquid iron outer core heats the base of the overlying mantle. Seismic tomography — imaging the Earth’s interior using the speed of earthquake waves — shows slow-velocity (hot) anomalies beneath major hotspots like Hawaii and Iceland extending hundreds to thousands of kilometres deep into the mantle, consistent with this deep-rooted origin.

Flood Basalts: The Plume Head’s Arrival

When a new plume first arrives at the base of the lithosphere, its head (which can be 1,000+ km wide) dumps an enormous amount of heat into the base of the lithosphere simultaneously, generating catastrophic volumes of basaltic magma. This produces a large igneous province (LIP) — also called a flood basalt — where hundreds of thousands of cubic kilometres of basalt erupt in geologically brief pulses of 1–3 million years. The Deccan Traps of India (~66 Ma), the Siberian Traps (~252 Ma), and the Columbia River Basalts of Washington/Oregon (~16 Ma) are all flood basalts associated with plume head arrivals. They have been linked to mass extinctions (the Siberian Traps with the end-Permian extinction, the Deccan Traps with the end-Cretaceous — though the asteroid impact takes most of the blame for the latter).

Three Diagnostic Contrasts: Hotspot vs. Boundary Volcanism

(1) Location: Hotspot volcanoes occur in the interior of plates, far from any boundary. Boundary volcanism is restricted to ridge crests or subduction zones. (2) Age pattern: Hotspot volcanism produces an age-progressive chain with one active volcano at the plume position. Subduction arc volcanism produces a belt of contemporaneous volcanoes all active at the same time. (3) Chemistry: Hotspot lavas are basaltic, low-silica, enriched in trace elements like strontium, lead, and neodymium that reflect a deep mantle source (ocean island basalt, OIB). Subduction-related lavas are andesitic to rhyolitic, silica-enriched from crustal contamination and fluid flux from the slab. Ridge basalts are depleted of these trace elements because the upper mantle source has already had much of its fusible component extracted by repeated melting.

Concept 7.2

Hawaii, Yellowstone, and Iceland: Three Faces of Hotspot Volcanism

Hawaii: The Paradigm Oceanic Hotspot

The Hawaiian island chain is the classic demonstration of hotspot mechanics. The island chain extends from the Big Island of Hawaii (currently active, formed in the last 0.4 million years) progressively northwest to Kauai (5.6 million years old), then continues as submerged, eroded seamounts (the Emperor Seamount Chain, extending to the Aleutian Trench). The entire chain stretches 5,800 km and represents 85 million years of Pacific Plate motion over the Hawaiian plume.

Calculating Pacific Plate Velocity from Island Ages

This is an elegant quantitative exercise. The distance from the Big Island (active, ~0 Ma) to Kauai (~5.6 Ma) is about 500 km. The plate velocity is therefore 500 km ÷ 5.6 Ma ≈ 9 cm/yr to the northwest — one of the fastest-moving plates on Earth. At the bend in the Emperor-Hawaiian chain (the “elbow” ~43 Ma ago), the direction of motion changed from more northward to the current northwest. This bend records a major change in the Pacific Plate’s motion direction around 43 million years ago, possibly related to the Himalayan collision initiating and changing the force balance on the Pacific Plate.

Yellowstone: The Continental Hotspot

When a mantle plume sits beneath thick continental crust instead of thin oceanic crust, the results are very different. The crust partially melts, producing silica-rich, extremely explosive rhyolitic magmas that erupt as supervolcanic calderas rather than gentle shield volcanoes. The Snake River Plain of Idaho is the track of the North American Plate moving southwest over the Yellowstone plume — a broad, flat plain of ancient rhyolitic and basaltic eruptions, with the youngest eruptions at Yellowstone National Park (Wyoming, currently at the leading edge of the plate over the plume). The three major Yellowstone caldera eruptions in the past 2.1 million years (each 1,000–2,500 times more powerful than the 1980 Mount St. Helens eruption) are among the largest volcanic events in Earth’s recent geological record.

Iceland: A Hotspot on a Ridge

Iceland is the unique case where a mantle plume sits directly beneath a mid-ocean ridge — the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The combination of decompression melting at the ridge plus the additional heat from the plume generates far more magma than a typical ridge segment, building Iceland above sea level. Iceland’s volcanism is therefore driven by two superimposed processes simultaneously, making it one of the most volcanically productive places on Earth per unit area. This dual nature also means Iceland’s lavas have a chemistry that is intermediate between typical ocean island basalt (hotspot) and mid-ocean ridge basalt (MORB) — a geochemical signature that confirms its dual origin.

Unit 8

Active Tectonics as Hazard: When Geology Affects Civilization

Everything we have studied in this lecture — plate boundaries, fault types, volcanic mechanisms — is not merely academic. These processes generate the world’s most destructive natural hazards: earthquakes that can kill hundreds of thousands of people in minutes and tsunamis that can devastate coastlines. Understanding plate tectonics directly informs how governments plan cities, build infrastructure, and warn populations. This final unit applies tectonic theory to the urgent question of hazard assessment.

Concept 8.1

Earthquake Hazard: The Tectonic Map Translated Into Risk

A seismic hazard map is, at its core, a plate tectonic map with probability added. Every high-hazard zone on such a map corresponds to an active plate boundary or a recently reactivated ancient fault. When the USGS produced its 2023 National Seismic Hazard Map, they were essentially asking: given what we know about where active faults are, how fast they move, and how they rupture, what is the probability of damaging ground shaking at each location in the next 50 or 100 years?

Reading the Hazard Map: Observation Questions

Why are Alaska, California, and Washington the highest-hazard states?

Alaska sits above the Aleutian Subduction Zone, where the Pacific Plate subducts beneath North America along the world’s longest subduction zone. The 1964 Alaska earthquake (M9.2) — the second-largest ever recorded — occurred here. Washington state sits above the Cascadia Subduction Zone, where the Juan de Fuca Plate subducts beneath North America. California sits on the right-lateral San Andreas fault system. All three are directly associated with active plate boundaries where large fault ruptures are inevitable.

What is that isolated high-hazard patch in the middle of the continent?

The isolated orange-yellow zone in Missouri, Arkansas, Tennessee, and Illinois corresponds to the New Madrid Seismic Zone — a failed continental rift from about 500 million years ago that never completed the rift-to-ocean transition. The ancient normal faults of this failed rift are being reactivated by modern compressional stresses in the North American plate interior. In the winter of 1811–1812, three earthquakes of magnitude 7.0–8.0 struck here, temporarily reversing the flow of the Mississippi River and causing widespread liquefaction. A comparable event today would cause catastrophic damage to densely populated, historically unprepared cities including Memphis, Nashville, and St. Louis.

The Cascadia Subduction Zone: “The Really Big One”

The Cascadia Subduction Zone off the coast of Oregon and Washington is arguably the most dangerous geological feature in North America that most people have never heard of. The Juan de Fuca Plate has been subducting beneath North America for millions of years, but the fault interface has been locked — no major rupture — for about 300 years, since the last great earthquake in January 1700 (documented in Japanese tsunami records). The locked fault is accumulating elastic strain that must eventually release. Scientists estimate that when the full fault ruptures, it will produce a M8.0–9.2 earthquake followed by a major Pacific Northwest tsunami. The hazard map’s elevated probabilities for Washington and Oregon reflect this known pending rupture.

Concept 8.2

Volcano Monitoring: Plate Tectonics Translated Into Early Warning

The Alaska Volcano Observatory (AVO) is a joint programme of the USGS, University of Alaska Fairbanks, and the Alaska Division of Geological and Geophysical Surveys. Its mission is to monitor the more than 50 active volcanoes of the Aleutian arc — a direct consequence of Pacific Plate subduction — and provide early warning of eruptions that could threaten aviation (aircraft regularly fly through the North Pacific corridor) and communities. The AVO illustrates how plate tectonic theory has a direct, life-saving operational application.

How Scientists Detect an Upcoming Eruption

Before most volcanic eruptions, the volcano provides detectable warning signs that monitoring networks are designed to catch. As magma rises toward the surface, it forces its way through rock, generating swarms of small earthquakes (volcanic tremor and volcano-tectonic earthquakes) that are picked up by seismometers. The injection of magma into the volcanic system causes the ground surface to inflate measurably — detected by GPS stations and satellite radar (InSAR) that can measure ground deformation to centimetre precision. Heated magma drives chemical reactions that release sulfur dioxide (SO₂), carbon dioxide, and hydrogen sulfide gases — gas sensors and satellite spectrometers measure these emissions continuously. Finally, infrared satellite sensors detect anomalous heat at the crater before any visible eruption. Together, these multi-parameter monitoring systems give scientists days to weeks of warning for most eruptions, enabling evacuations that have saved thousands of lives.

The AVO Alert Level System: From Theory to Practice

The four alert levels used by AVO and all USGS Volcano Observatories (Green/Normal, Yellow/Advisory, Orange/Watch, Red/Warning) are based on observable precursors: Green = background seismicity, normal gas output, no deformation. Yellow = elevated seismicity and/or gas emissions above baseline; volcano is showing signs of unrest but no imminent eruption. Orange = significant unrest; eruption possible within weeks, or eruption occurring but minor. Red = eruption occurring with significant lava, ash plume, or pyroclastic activity; aviation and ground hazards immediate. Aviation authorities respond to Orange and Red by rerouting aircraft. Civil authorities begin evacuations at Orange and mandatory evacuations at Red. This graduated system — built on decades of volcanological research and seismic monitoring — translates scientific observations into actionable public safety decisions.

Synthesis and Integration

All Boundaries in One Cross-Section

The diagram below is the master integrative reference for plate tectonics. Every boundary type, structural feature, and volcanic form is shown together in a single panoramic cross-section. Take time to trace each element: on the left, a subduction zone with its trench, volcanic arc, and Benioff zone earthquakes deepening toward the arc. In the centre, a mid-ocean ridge (divergent boundary) with its central rift and spreading magnetic stripes. On the right, a continental rift zone (young divergent boundary) with normal faults and small volcanoes. And independently, a mantle plume generating a hotspot shield volcano unrelated to any boundary. This single image encodes the complete plate tectonics vocabulary.

Cross-Section Construction Exercise: From Map to Structure

The map below shows Central America and the Caribbean with multiple plates visible: the Pacific Plate (large, west), the Cocos Plate (between Pacific Ridge and Central America), the Caribbean Plate (central), and to the east the North American and Nubian plates separated by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. A transect line X–Y runs from the Pacific Coast of Central America to the eastern Caribbean near the Lesser Antilles arc. Your task is to mentally construct, then verify, a complete cross-section along that line, naming every boundary, trench, arc, and Benioff zone you cross.

👀 Reveal the Complete Cross-Section Solution
From X (west) to Y (east): (1) East Pacific Rise — spreading centre, Cocos and Pacific plates diverging. (2) Cocos Plate interior — moving east at ~9 cm/yr. (3) Middle America Trench — where Cocos Plate begins subducting beneath the Caribbean Plate; trench teeth point west (Caribbean overriding). (4) Benioff Zone — earthquakes deepening eastward under Central America. (5) Central American volcanic arc (volcanoes of Guatemala, Costa Rica, Nicaragua) — positioned above the flux-melting zone at ~100 km slab depth. (6) Caribbean Plate interior — oceanic plateau, generally tectonically quiet, moving ~2 cm/yr east relative to South America. (7) Lesser Antilles Trench — where the Atlantic/North American oceanic plate subducts westward beneath the Caribbean Plate. (8) Lesser Antilles volcanic arc (Martinique, St. Vincent, Montserrat) — above flux-melting zone. (9) Eastern edge of Caribbean Plate — transform and spreading segments bordering the Nubian Plate.

Master Reference

Complete Glossary of Key Terms

Every bolded term from Lecture 4, defined with its observational basis. The goal is to understand where each term came from, not just what it means.

Accretionary WedgeA mass of sediment and oceanic crustal fragments scraped off a subducting plate and piled up at the subduction zone trench; grows like snow in front of a snowplow.
AnticlineA fold in which rock layers arch upward; oldest rocks are exposed in the core. Forms under compressional stress.
AsthenosphereThe ductile, partially molten upper mantle (~100–660 km depth) on which rigid lithospheric plates move; solid on short timescales but flows over millions of years.
Benioff Zone (Wadati–Benioff)The inclined zone of earthquakes generated within a subducting slab; its geometry traces the descending plate from trench to depths of 700 km, proving the physical existence of the slab.
Brittle–Ductile TransitionThe depth (~10–15 km in continental crust) below which rock responds to stress by flowing (ductile) rather than fracturing (brittle); temperature and pressure controlled.
Continental DriftWegener’s 1912 hypothesis that continents once formed Pangea and have since moved apart. Supported by geometric fit, fossils, rock belts, and paleoclimate but lacked mechanism until seafloor spreading was discovered.
Decompression MeltingPartial melting caused by pressure reduction as rock rises toward the surface; the primary melting mechanism at mid-ocean ridges.
Deformation FrontThe leading edge of active fold-and-thrust deformation in a fold belt; marks where the compressional stress front has reached.
Divergent MarginA plate boundary where two plates move apart; creates new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges or rift valleys in continents. Dominated by tensional stress and normal faulting.
Elastic Rebound TheoryThe mechanism of earthquake generation: stress accumulates in locked fault rocks (elastic deformation), eventually exceeds frictional resistance, and releases catastrophically as seismic waves (the “rebound”).
Flood Basalt / Large Igneous ProvinceCatastrophic eruptions of hundreds of thousands of km³ of basalt in geologically short periods; associated with mantle plume head arrivals; linked to mass extinctions.
Flux MeltingPartial melting triggered by water released from a subducting slab into the overlying mantle wedge; lowers melting point of peridotite and generates arc magmas. The key mechanism behind subduction-related volcanism.
Fold-and-Thrust BeltA zone of compressional deformation where stacked thrust sheets and folds shorten and thicken the crust; found at the leading edges of mountain belts and collision zones.
FootwallThe block of rock beneath a fault plane; does not move relative to the hanging wall in fault classification.
Foreland BasinA depression formed by lithospheric flexure under the weight of a thrust belt; fills with sediment eroded from the growing mountain range above.
Fracture ZoneThe inactive extension of an oceanic transform fault beyond the ridge offsets; a topographic scar with no seismicity, as both sides are on the same plate.
GrabenA down-dropped crustal block bounded by parallel normal faults; forms the floor of rift valleys.
HangingwallThe block above a fault plane; its direction of motion (up = reverse; down = normal) is the primary diagnostic criterion for fault classification.
HorstAn elevated crustal block bounded by normal faults; forms the ridges flanking rift valley grabens.
HotspotAn isolated volcanic centre above a stationary mantle plume, producing an age-progressive volcanic chain as the plate moves over it; unrelated to any plate boundary.
Island ArcA curved chain of stratovolcanoes built on oceanic crust above an oceanic-oceanic subduction zone; characterized by andesitic to basaltic eruptions from flux melting.
IsostasyGravitational equilibrium of crustal blocks floating on the denser mantle; thicker crust stands higher and has a deeper root, like an iceberg.
Large Igneous Province (LIP)See Flood Basalt.
Left-Lateral FaultA strike-slip fault where the block on the opposite side has moved to the left when viewed from either side.
LithosphereThe rigid outer shell of Earth (crust + uppermost mantle, ~0–100 km depth); broken into tectonic plates; mechanically distinct from the ductile asthenosphere below.
Magnetic AnomalyA departure from the expected magnetic field strength caused by remanent magnetism in seafloor basalt; the symmetric stripe pattern is one of the four lines of evidence for seafloor spreading.
Mantle PlumeA buoyant column of anomalously hot mantle material rising from depth (possibly the core-mantle boundary), penetrating the lithosphere and generating hotspot volcanism at the surface.
Moho (Mohorovičić Discontinuity)The seismically defined boundary between crust and mantle; marked by a sharp increase in P-wave velocity from ~6 km/s (crust) to ~8 km/s (mantle).
New Madrid Seismic ZoneA zone of elevated seismicity in the central USA corresponding to a 500 Ma failed rift, now reactivated by modern intraplate stresses; a reminder that ancient tectonic structures remain hazardous.
Normal FaultA fault where the hangingwall has moved downward; produced by tensional stress; common at divergent margins and rift zones.
Ocean Island Basalt (OIB)Basaltic lava erupted at oceanic hotspots; chemically enriched in trace elements (Sr, Nd, Pb) reflecting a deep mantle source; distinctive from both MORB and arc lavas.
OphioliteA fragment of ancient oceanic crust and upper mantle thrust onto a continent at a suture zone; direct evidence of ancient ocean floor now on land.
Orogen / OrogenesisA belt of deformed, metamorphosed, and uplifted rocks recording a mountain-building event; orogenesis is the process of building mountains through crustal thickening at convergent margins.
PangeaThe Permian-Triassic supercontinent (~300–175 Ma) comprising all modern continents; its breakup by rifting and seafloor spreading opened the Atlantic, Indian, and Southern oceans.
Passive MarginA tectonically quiet continental edge far from any active plate boundary, subsiding slowly under sediment load; the US East Coast is a classic example.
Ridge PushThe gravitational force pushing lithospheric plates away from elevated, thermally buoyant mid-ocean ridges; a contributing (though not dominant) force in plate motion.
Reverse FaultA fault where the hangingwall has moved upward against gravity; produced by compressional stress; builds mountains at convergent margins.
Rift ValleyAn elongated depression formed by tensional normal faulting as a continent begins to pull apart; the initial stage of future ocean basin formation.
Right-Lateral FaultA strike-slip fault where the opposite block has moved to the right; the San Andreas Fault is the classic example.
Seafloor SpreadingThe continuous creation of new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges and its lateral movement outward; proposed by Harry Hess ~1960 and confirmed by magnetic anomalies, age patterns, and seismicity.
Slab PullThe dominant force driving plate motion; the negative buoyancy of cold, dense subducting oceanic lithosphere pulls the attached plate into the mantle. Plates with active subduction margins move faster.
Strike-Slip FaultA fault with predominantly horizontal motion; formed by shear stress; classified as right-lateral or left-lateral based on relative displacement direction.
SubductionThe descent of dense (oceanic) lithosphere beneath less-dense lithosphere into the mantle at a convergent boundary; generates trenches, Benioff zones, and arc volcanism via flux melting.
Suture ZoneThe linear belt of deformed, mixed lithologies marking where two formerly separate continents have collided and welded together; often contains ophiolites and high-pressure metamorphic rocks.
SynclineA fold in which rock layers arch downward; youngest rocks are in the core. Forms under the same compressional stress that creates anticlines.
Thrust FaultA low-angle (<45° dip) reverse fault; fundamental in building mountain belts and fold-and-thrust belts; megathrust faults at subduction zones generate the world’s largest earthquakes.
Transform BoundaryA plate boundary where plates slide laterally past each other along strike-slip faults; no crust created or destroyed; produces shallow, potentially large-magnitude earthquakes.
TrenchThe deep linear depression (>6,000 m) where oceanic lithosphere bends and descends into the mantle at a subduction zone; the deepest topography on Earth’s surface.
Triple JunctionA point where three plate boundaries meet; constrained to specific geometrically stable configurations; the Afar Triple Junction (three divergent boundaries) is a modern example.
Volcanic ArcA chain of volcanoes parallel to and above a subduction zone, formed by flux melting of the mantle wedge triggered by water release from the descending slab.
Volcanic TremorContinuous, low-frequency seismic vibration caused by magma moving through cracks; a key precursor signal used by volcanologists to detect magma ascent before eruptions.
Wadati–Benioff ZoneSee Benioff Zone.
Wilson CycleThe recurring ~400–600 Ma cycle of ocean basin opening (rifting and seafloor spreading) and closing (subduction and continental collision), first described by J. Tuzo Wilson.
XenolithA fragment of deep crustal or mantle rock incorporated into and carried to the surface by a rising magma; provides direct physical samples of Earth’s otherwise inaccessible interior, confirming seismic inferences.
